chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Ray Nance: salesman, 'Kitty on Toast', and being talked into joining Duke
summary: Nance played violin and trumpet, recorded Kitty on Toast with Horace, and was loyal to the band until persuaded to leave for Ellington after Duke heard him in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Sure. Makes a difference. What about Ray Nance?

Ray Nance. Nance was quite a seller, a salesman, music-wise. He was (inaudible). As you know, he played the violin, for (inaudible), played it well. He did some things for Duke, and he recorded a tune with me and John Hammond, the great John Hammond, the critic, (inaudible) -- "Kitty on Toast," I remember, and it was a takeoff -- the chords were like they call it (inaudible) "Honeysuckle Rose," only diminished things, and Ray would run them, and I used to (inaudible) thing (inaudible) you know, and the would hold the diminished thing and Ray would run through saxophone section (inaudible), and that was a great thing that he did. And, of course, he had a nice tone on trumpet. And, of course, you know what happened on "A Train" with Duke Ellington. (Inaudible). That beautiful solo is legend.

(Inaudible). But Ray was from Chicago, and he used to play on the South Side there for the great Ben Escola, and he played on the North Side with that 5100 Club (inaudible) that I was telling you about that I think Danny Thomas was there. And this is where Duke first heard him, and he came out and offered him a job. Do you know Ray turned him down? Man, when we heard about it, we got so mad, we had to almost quit speaking to him before he would go. He was that loyal to the group, you know. Oh, he played, and he could really sell, he could dance, and I knew his first wife real well. She was a singer. Melrose Rose was her name. And she didn't want him to leave, I think. This is why he felt that way, besides being happy where he was, and he played seven nights a week. But nevertheless we finally
talked Ray into going. You know the story after that.
